name: West Papua
summary_text: West Papua stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, add their own criminalisation, but West Papua is not among them.  The dominant risk in this province is the conduct of the security forces rather than any trans-specific provision. A report of 22 July 2025 by the Asia-Pacific Solidarity Network records 138 acts of torture or other ill-treatment against people in detention by police and military in Maybrat and the Central Highlands areas of West Papua, covering the period through early 2025. Most victims were male and under 24; seven were female, seven were minors aged 15 to 17. The report's finding is near-total impunity, summarised as impunity, secrecy and silence. Any visitor held or questioned by officers in the province faces an accountability environment in which abuse is unlikely to be answered for.  Military activity in the province has intensified. The Papua human-rights monitor's quarterly report for the third quarter of 2025 records a notable increase in military deployments and operations in West Papua's highland regions since August 2025. Police in Sorong arrested more than a dozen protest participants in August 2025. On 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in Agats, Asmat Regency, alongside ongoing displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous Papuans.  No trans-specific finding is recorded for West Papua in these sources. The general security-force pattern nonetheless amplifies exposure for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor, since stops, document checks and detention in the province are handled by units already documented committing ill-treatment with impunity.

name: Isle of Man
summary_text: The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the Isle of Man. Local law governs, and United Kingdom measures reach the island only by Order in Council.  The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency. Its parliament, Tynwald, frames these questions through its own bills rather than through inherited Westminster statute, so the island's record must be read on its own terms.  Partner recognition is established. Same-sex marriage took effect on the island after Royal Assent of the Marriage and Civil Partnership Act, reported on 28 July 2016, and the first conversion of a civil partnership into a marriage was completed within days of entry into force. Civil partnerships, legal since 2011, convert without a second ceremony, which indicates a routine registration process rather than discretionary approval.  The primary legislative record of that reform sits in Tynwald Hansard for 26 April 2016, which records the Legislative Council's Third Reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016 alongside consideration of the Equality Bill 2016. The reform also had stated political sponsorship: on 9 June 2015 Chief Minister Allan Bell publicly backed same-sex marriage and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition, a commitment that preceded the 2016 Act.  Non-discrimination protection on the island was first legislated in the employment sphere. On 30 November 2005 the House of Keys adopted an amendment to the Employment Bill, tabled by Onchan MHK Peter Karran, barring dismissal of gay and lesbian employees on sexual-orientation grounds and aligning the island with United Kingdom human-rights law.  Nothing in this inventory documents a gender-recognition procedure, identity-document marker rules, entry or visa screening that could disclose a trans visitor's status, hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, or facility access rules. Those questions are not evidenced here rather than shown to be absent from Manx law, and a visitor should treat them as open.
